bio: I’m Jordan Oleson-Graves, an Atlanta-based artist, designer, and educator creating work with code. My journey began at SCAD with a BFA in Motion Media Design, where discovering abstract animation redirected my passion from commercial art toward open experimentation. After exploring physical craft and 3D printing, learning to code transformed my creative process, allowing me to bring years of ideas to life, from code-generated knitwear to responsive LED environments. Following an MS in Digital Media at Georgia Tech centered on craft and CS education, I now teach high school Computer Science to help students build their own ideas, while pursuing my MFA in Painting back at SCAD.
statement: Curiosity drives my work, rooted in a time when growing up alongside technology made it easy to see how things actually worked. As a child with undiagnosed nearsightedness, I sat inches from the family television, just as entertained by the stories on screen as I was by watching distinct bands of red, green, and blue light blend together when I stepped back. Later, learning HTML and CSS happened almost by accident, a quiet byproduct of customizing early social media pages. Today, as digital tools progress into sleek interfaces and pervasive generative artificial intelligence, those underlying mechanics have been hidden, and modern technology no longer inspires that same casual curiosity. I choose to pull those computational foundations back into the light, celebrating a distinct artistic language born from early display limitations.

My practice is entirely medium-agnostic. Every idea begins in code, but its physical form is chosen based on the experience it needs to create, whether through responsive LEDs, textiles, printmaking, or kinetic sculpture. Working with algorithmic rules, I treat my process as a modular playground, writing programs to explore a vast field of potential visual outcomes. I share this personal exploration across physical series that communicate how key variables change, digital co-creation tools that let others manipulate parameters themselves, and installations that respond dynamically to bodily movement. Ultimately, these systems invite viewers to step inside my process, offering a playful environment where they can share in my path of visual discovery.
